claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit intermittent, serrated stress-strain responses at elevated temperatures.
The serrations arise from avalanches of collectively slipping weak zones.
Avalanche slip occurs when the applied strain rate exceeds the thermal healing rate of localized weak zones.
Avalanche slip causes jerky thermoelastic behavior in addition to jerky mechanical deformation.
The specimens have a homogeneous microstructure containing local slip-weak zones.
Cold rolling and annealing are suitable standard routes for producing the proposed homogeneous weak-zone-containing state.
Systematically changing strain rate and temperature modulates the balance between loading and thermally activated healing.
The relevant structural mediator is the distribution and healing kinetics of weak microstructural zones that serve as avalanche-slip sites.
Increasing temperature promotes faster healing or reordering of weak zones relative to the applied strain rate.
Faster healing refines collective slip events and makes deformation smoother.
Higher strain rates or lower temperatures will produce more pronounced stress serrations and sudden stress drops.
Higher temperatures or lower strain rates will reduce serration amplitude and frequency and produce smoother deformation.
Conventional alloys with fewer principal elements exhibit more uniform deformation without marked serrations under comparable conditions.
Tests from approximately 673 K to 1073 K, including strain rates around 0.001 s^-1, cover the relevant kinetic regime.
Diffusion-controlled softening does not dominate below approximately 1073 K.
The quantitative transition thresholds and the activation energy of healing are not yet established.
A lack of systematic temperature- or strain-rate dependence in serration amplitude or frequency would falsify the proposed kinetic-competition mechanism.
Observation of similar serration behavior in conventional-alloy controls under identical conditions would falsify the claimed distinction from the baseline.
